cultivar: Lavandula angustifolia (true or English lavender), the only one worth drinking; the hybrid lavandin grown for oil is too camphorous
processing: Flower spikes are cut at full bloom, dried in shade and the florets rubbed from the stems and sifted; culinary grades are selected for low camphor and intact colour.
harvest_season: Late June to August, cut at full bloom in dry weather; the whole year's supply is dried then.
appearance_dry: Tiny grey-violet to deep purple dried florets like little beads, with a few bits of stem.
appearance_liquor: Pale grey-yellow with a faint pink tint, clear.
appearance_wet: Softened dull-purple florets with a strong perfumed smell.
taste_profile: Perfumed and floral with a sweet, herbaceous body and a hint of rosemary-like camphor; delicate as a pinch, soapy and bitter as a spoonful.

brewing.notes: A level teaspoon per cup at most, just-boiled water, 3–4 minutes; more lavender or more time tastes of soap. Most people prefer it blended: a pinch in chamomile, in Earl Grey, in mint, or in warm milk with honey.

vintage_note: Sold as the current summer's flowers and best within a year, since the colour fades from purple to grey-brown and the scent turns dusty. Look for 'lavande fine', 'true lavender', 'Lavandula angustifolia' or 'culinary grade' on the label; cheaper lavandin flowers are larger, paler and harsh with camphor, and lavender sold for sachets or crafts is not always clean enough to drink. Provence, Bulgaria and England are the usual origins.
description:
Lavender is a seasoning more than a tea: a pinch of the dried purple florets turns a pot of chamomile, mint or Earl Grey into something perfumed and summery, while a whole spoonful on its own tastes like a bar of soap. The best flowers for the cup come from true lavender grown high in Provence, not from the bigger hybrid lavandin fields that supply the perfume industry.

The spikes are cut at full bloom in high summer and dried in shade, and the florets are rubbed off and sifted. Culinary lavender is selected for low camphor and good colour, and the species matters: true lavender is sweet and floral, lavandin is sharp and medicinal, and the label should say which.

Brewed alone, a teaspoon in a cup for three or four minutes gives a pale, delicate infusion that is floral, slightly herbaceous and sweet; go beyond that and bitterness and soapiness take over, which is why most people have had a bad lavender tea. Blended it is wonderful: with chamomile at bedtime, with mint, in warm milk with honey, or in a London Fog, which is Earl Grey, steamed milk and a touch of lavender.

Buy small amounts of deep-purple culinary-grade flowers from the latest harvest, and store them in the dark. There is no vintage, but the difference between this year's flowers and three-year-old ones is the difference between perfume and dust.

It has traditionally been drunk as a calming evening infusion; whatever you make of that, think of it as the herb equivalent of a drop of orange-blossom water: a little goes a very long way.
history:
True lavender is a shrub native to the Mediterranean basin, called English lavender although it is not native to England. It is commonly grown as an ornamental and for its fragrance, and it is among the herbs kept in gardens for tea.

Little is documented about when lavender became a drink in its own right. It is best thought of as a garden infusion and a flavouring for blends, without a known point of origin or a named maker behind it.
